query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor reactive element that promotes controlled tribo‐oxidation into the CoCrFeNi matrix will induce an in-situ formation of an adaptive, lubricious oxide nanocomposite (glaze) layer during sliding, thereby maintaining a low friction coefficient and wear rate from room temperature up to high operating temperatures. This occurs via the formation of a self-renewing oxide film that mediates friction reduction.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with its typical solid-solution phase(s) that shows increasing wear and friction variations under high-temperature sliding.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small, carefully optimized quantity of a reactive trace element into the alloy composition. This additive is intended to act as a catalyst for in-situ tribochemical reactions.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient air using a ball-on-disk configuration under moderate loads over a temperature range from room temperature up to high operating temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuously regenerated, ultrafine, amorphous-crystalline oxide nanocomposite (glaze) layer that forms at the sliding interface during operation.
generation.mechanism: The reactive additive facilitates controlled tribo-oxidation during sliding, promoting the in-situ formation of a lubricious surface film that dissipates frictional stresses and suppresses wear mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi, the intervention is predicted to yield a substantially lower and more stable friction coefficient and reduced wear rates across the entire temperature span, achieving wear resistance similar to or better than systems that develop self-lubricating tribolayers.
generation.baseline: The standard CoCrFeNi alloy without any reactive additive, which typically suffers from increased wear and friction variability—especially at higher temperatures—due to oxidation and structural softening at the sliding interface.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under ambient atmospheric conditions with moderate sliding loads (e.g., 5 N) and in the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Behavior outside these conditions (e.g., very high loads, non-ambient environments) may not follow the same trend.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal identity and amount of the reactive trace element are not definitively known, so its precise concentration and potential impact on overall phase stability require further experimental calibration. Additionally, the longevity and continuous regeneration of the glaze layer under cyclic wear conditions remain to be fully confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloy samples: one set of conventional CoCrFeNi and another with a minor addition of the chosen reactive trace element. Perform systematic ball-on-disk sliding tests at defined loads in ambient air across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Ensure all other processing parameters are identical.
measurements: Record the coefficient of friction continuously during sliding.
Measure wear rates (e.g., via profilometry to quantify wear volume).
Characterize the worn surfaces using SEM, EDS, and XPS to determine the presence, continuity, and nature of any oxide nanocomposite layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reactive-additive modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the temperature range compared to the baseline alloy, or if no continuous adaptive glaze layer is detected, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude.
